findings.quote: connected objects move with the same acceleration while the rope stays tight
findings.problem: False for the case named in the same paragraph: a rope over an ideal pulley. Over a pulley the connected objects have the same size of acceleration but not the same direction (in an Atwood machine one mass speeds up going up while the other goes down; a table block moves sideways while the hanging block moves down). The lesson treats acceleration as a vector with a direction (line on the second law, and Example #6, 'The accelerations point in opposite directions'), so 'the same acceleration' here tells the student the directions match. A student who gives both masses the same signed a gets a wrong answer in any pulley problem.
findings.source: Checklist B01; reader-rules.md 'Added after the Sol audit' (test each general statement against a known exception); OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.1 Example 6.5 (Atwood machine: accelerations equal in magnitude)

findings.quote: Split any arrow that is not along an axis into components
findings.problem: The lesson teaches splitting an angled force into F cos(theta) and F sin(theta) here and in Core Concept, and says an angled push changes the friction balance and the normal force, but no worked example ever splits an applied force. Example #11 uses a weight split that the lesson states as a ready result, not this method. The standard application, a box pulled or pushed at an angle on a level floor, where N = mg - F sin(theta) and the friction uses that N, is a distinct case from the incline and from the vertical pushes of Example #4. A student who meets it will likely use N = mg, the very error Trap #4 warns about.
findings.source: Checklist L18; writer-rules.md lead ruling 1 (standard application of a skill in the lesson's goal); brief: 'add an explicit isolated-object force construction with components before combined force use'

findings.quote: Treat them together as one object of mass $3+2=5\,\mathrm{kg}$.
findings.problem: The solution then uses only the 20 N pull on the group and leaves out the rope tension, but never says why: the rope's pull back on A and its pull forward on B are inside the group, equal and opposite, so they cancel and only outside forces count. The Speed Tricks section recommends this whole-group method, yet the lesson nowhere explains how it works. The base taught that a free-body diagram may isolate an object or a system and shows only external forces; the rewrite cut 'system' and 'external', so the reason is now missing.
findings.source: Checklist L26 and L19 (step skipped); base 7032eec5 Free-Body Diagrams: 'isolates one chosen object/system and shows the external forces acting on that object/system'
